Figure 1 :  PrimeSim.  (a)  The midtraining corpus: roughly
30.1K hours of curated robot data spanning humanoid, dual-arm, single-arm and
handheld UMI  [ 14 ,  3 ]  platforms, mixing real and simulated footage.  (b)  The
model is conditioned on a language prompt, a unified action representation over
head, torso, waist, end-effector, gripper and chassis, and three camera views,
and predicts future frames; post-training makes generation autoregressive with
a selected KV-cache memory at four denoising steps.  (c)  Capabilities:
fidelity against prior systems, action following measured against simulation
ground truth, few-shot adaptation to an unseen embodiment, and use as a
simulator: success rate in PrimeSim predicts success rate in the LIBERO  [ 51 ]  physics
simulator with  r = 0.99 r=0.99 , so policies can be trained in the model and
the result carried back to the robot.

Figure 2 :  Overview of the data pipeline. Raw demonstrations from
teleoperation, UMI, and simulation are converted through four stages:
video quality filtering, action quality filtering, action preprocessing,
and data alignment. Each stage lists the operations applied to the incoming
data. The pipeline produces a unified corpus of 30,110 hours across 20
dataset families and 22 robot platforms
(Table  12 ).

Figure 3 :  Overview of the PrimeSim training corpus: 30,110 hours, 2.38B
frames and 1.52M episodes from 1,773 repositories over 22 robot platforms, at
an 84:16 real-to-simulated ratio.  Left:  the task-category and
embodiment distributions.  Right:  example frames from each of the
five embodiment classes.

Figure 4 :  The PrimeSim model architecture.  Left:  the whole system,
including the input data modalities, the VAE, the text encoder and the
PrimeSim decoder.  Right:  the action conditioning mechanisms, a
framewise attention mask and a frame-action adaptor.

Figure 5 :  General action representation in PrimeSim, covering single-arm,
bimanual, UMI, and wheeled humanoid embodiments.

Figure 6 :  Overview of the post-training pipeline, from the midtrained
base model through the four adaptation stages to the deployed simulator.

Table 1 :  WorldSimProbe results on LIBERO  [ 51 ] , against five open-source
action-conditioned world models. T1–T3 measure action realization (local action
calibration, global trajectory coverage, action-source behavior preservation);
T4–T5 measure interaction response (interaction grounding, interaction dynamics).
Bold marks the best value per suite; higher is better. PrimeSim leads four of the
five, all but local action calibration.

Table 2 :  EWMBench scores. Higher is better; Overall is the sum of the eight
dimensions. The first block is action-conditioned like ours; the second
block is instruction- or text-conditioned and therefore not iso-protocol
with ours (e.g. Thinker-WM generates at 5 FPS upsampled to 30 FPS for
scoring). GE-Sim rows are computed from the published Genie Envisioner
simulation evaluation  [ 50 ] , aligned to the standard
EWMBench column names. Thinker-WM, Qwen-RobotWorld, LVP, Sora2 and Kling26
rows are as reported on the same 21-episode split in  [ 24 ] ,
compiled there from  [ 95 ] .  † EnerVerse-FT is from
the EWMBench paper’s own evaluation  [ 93 ] .
 ‡ Thinker-WM (action-cond.) conditions on the ground-truth action
sequence; only its motion dimensions and Overall are
reported  [ 24 ] , averaged over the evaluated checkpoints.

Table 3 :  Inference throughput on a single NVIDIA A100-80GB (bfloat16),
measured as steady-state wall-clock throughput per autoregressive chunk under
each method’s released inference recipe. TempFPS counts rollout time steps
per second; ViewFPS counts each camera view as one frame and coincides with
TempFPS for single-view models. Rows are not matched in resolution, horizon
or denoising steps. PrimeSim is measured at  288 × 384 288\times 384  per view under the
RoboTwin 2.0 Stage-3 contract (33-frame windows, continuous KV, 32 usable
frames per window), a different geometry from the  192 × 256 192\times 256  setting of
the quality evaluations above.  † CausalWM is text- and
first-frame-conditioned, not action-conditioned.

Table 4 :  Few-shot adaptation to held-out embodiments. Both initialisations are
finetuned under an identical recipe with single-trajectory batches at a batch
size of 1 and a learning rate of  3 × 10 − 5 3\times 10^{-5} , and neither receives an
embodiment identifier or any embodiment-specific parameters. Entries are gradient steps to an
action-following rollout, meaning one in which the arm tracks the commanded
trajectory and the scene responds to the motion actually realized.
 † No action-following rollout was reached within this budget.

(a)   xArm 7 , midtrained, 200 gradient steps. (b)   xArm 7 , pretrained backbone, 2000 gradient steps. (c)   ViperX 300 , midtrained, 100 gradient steps. (d)   ViperX 300 , pretrained backbone, 2000 gradient steps. (e)   Original Stanford UMI gripper  [ 14 ] , midtrained, 200
gradient steps. (f)   Original Stanford UMI gripper  [ 14 ] , pretrained backbone,
2000 gradient steps. Figure 7 :  Few-shot adaptation to unseen embodiments. Each pair shows the
midtrained model above the pretrained backbone for one platform held out
from training: a single 7-DoF arm ( xArm 7 ) drawn from Open
X-Embodiment  [ 17 ] , a bimanual platform ( ViperX 300 , as used by
ALOHA  [ 98 ] ) and the original Stanford UMI gripper  [ 14 ] . Similar
embodiments do occur in the corpus, and they are what make
transfer possible at all, since a wholly alien platform would leave nothing to
build on. They are still new embodiments, however, and adaptation between
embodiments does not happen for free: each brings its own kinematics, camera
mounting and data distribution, which have to be acquired rather than
inherited. All initialisations are finetuned
under an identical recipe with single-trajectory batches at a batch size of 1,
and none receives an embodiment identifier or any embodiment-specific
parameters. The midtrained model reaches an action-following rollout within
100 to 200 gradient steps on all three platforms. The pretrained backbone,
which must initialise the action-conditioning and multiview modules from
scratch, does not reach the same regime even at ten to twenty times that
budget.
(a)   xArm 7 , midtrained, 200 gradient steps.
(b)   xArm 7 , pretrained backbone, 2000 gradient steps.
(c)   ViperX 300 , midtrained, 100 gradient steps.
(d)   ViperX 300 , pretrained backbone, 2000 gradient steps.

(e)   Original Stanford UMI gripper  [ 14 ] , midtrained, 200
gradient steps.

(f)   Original Stanford UMI gripper  [ 14 ] , pretrained backbone,
2000 gradient steps.

(a)   Before adaptation: zero-shot. (b)   After 200 gradient steps at batch size 1. Figure 8 :  Zero-shot and few-shot generation on an unseen setting and camera
pose. Both subfigures show the  AgileX Piper  bimanual arm on XVLA
 [ 100 ] , held out of pre-training entirely: the embodiment is in the
corpus, but the scene, the garments and the camera placements are not. Rows are
cameras (head, left wrist, right wrist) and columns are seven frames sampled
uniformly from a single rollout. (a) Without adaptation the model controls the
arms and renders the cloth, but the generated cloth state drifts from the
commanded action once the motion becomes contact-rich. (b) After 200 gradient
steps the arm trajectories and the cloth deformation track the commanded
actions much more closely and the three views stay mutually consistent, so most
of the cost of the transfer is recovered.
(a)   Before adaptation: zero-shot.
(b)   After 200 gradient steps at batch size 1.

Table 5 :  Zero-shot transfer to a held-out dataset. Both rows share the
checkpoint, sampler (50 steps, seed 42) and metrics at  192 × 256 192\times 256  over
three jointly generated views; only the data differs. XR2  [ 82 ]  is held-out episodes
of repositories seen in pre-training; XVLA is excluded and differs in scene,
garments and camera placement. Means  ± \pm  std over eight validation windows.
SSIM is not comparable across the two datasets, so only PSNR and LPIPS should
be read as a degradation.

Table 6 :  Distillation results. Stage 1 is the causal autoregressive teacher at
50 sampling steps. Stage 2 applies causal KV consistency distillation and
Stage 3 causal KV distribution matching distillation (DMD), both reducing
inference to 4 steps.

Table 7 :  Long-horizon generation quality averaged over ten held-out RoboTwin 2.0
episodes. Stage 3 uses fixed-length self-rollout training, while Stage 4
extends self-rollout training to complete episodes. The Stage 4 result uses the rolling  ( 3 + 18 ) (3+18)  cache configuration.
Table 8 :  KV-cache organization ablation for long-horizon generation.

Figure 9 :  (a)  Each point is one OpenVLA-OFT policy, evaluated on the
same 300 LIBERO-Spatial initial states in the world model (x) and in the
LIBERO simulator (y). The dotted line marks perfect agreement; points above
it mean the world model under-estimates the policy.  (b)  Success rate
of the SFT policy before and after 200 steps of GRPO post-training inside
PrimeSim, measured in the simulator (solid) and in PrimeSim (hatched).

Table 9 :  Ablation study on action representation. Best result per metric in
 bold .  ↑ \uparrow : higher is better;  ↓ \downarrow : lower is better.

(a)   (b)   Figure 10 :  Counterfactual action following on LIBERO. Each row shows seven
frames sampled uniformly from a single PrimeSim rollout, generated
conditional on an action sequence rather than a task prompt. Our evaluation
is built on counterfactual commands, meaning action trajectories that do not
correspond to the demonstrated behaviour. Faithful generation therefore
requires the model to respond to the commanded motion rather than replay the
recorded one. Static scene elements remain stable across the rollout while
the commanded motion is carried out, indicating that the generated future is
driven by the action rather than by visual plausibility alone.

Table 10 :  Ablation study on action conditioning. The  Baseline  column
uses vanilla cross-attention for framewise conditioning and Adaptive LayerNorm
(AdaLN) for the adapter;  Ours  uses modified cross-attention and
token fusion and shifting, respectively. The final row combines both
mechanisms. Higher PSNR is better.

Figure 11 :  Joint multiview generation. Rows are cameras, from top to bottom
head, left wrist and right wrist; columns are seven frames sampled uniformly
across a single 33-frame PrimeSim rollout. The three views are generated
together under a single action sequence rather than independently, and all
respond to the same commanded motion. The wrist views change most over the
interval, consistent with their proximity to the manipulation, while the head
view tracks the arms throughout.

Table 11 :  Ablation study on multiview consistency. Components are added
incrementally from naive frame concatenation. Best result in  bold .

Figure 12 :  Memory under occlusion.  Five frames from a single
RoboTwin 2.0 rollout, head camera. The arm sweeps across the workspace and its hand
passes in front of the shoe in the lower left (fourth frame), so the shoe leaves
the camera’s view entirely. When the hand clears, the shoe is present again at
the same position, scale and orientation rather than being re-invented or
dropped. Each window is conditioned on a selected KV-cache memory rather than on
the previous frame alone, so an object occluded for several seconds is carried
forward instead of being lost when it re-enters view.

Figure 13 :  Cloth manipulation rollouts, seven frames sampled uniformly
from each. All three are AgiBot G2 humanoid episodes shown from the head camera:
a white cloth on a bamboo table beside a metal bowl (top two rows), and a blue
cloth on a bedding surface with a folded garment to its right (bottom row). The
garment deforms continuously across each rollout and stays distinguishable from
the surface beneath it rather than dissolving into the background, which is the
failure mode deformable objects expose over long horizons.

Figure 14 :  Generated rollouts on two EWMBench tasks, the qualitative companion
of Table  2  (Sec.  4.1.2 ). Each row shows
seven frames sampled uniformly from a single rollout, generated open-loop at
10 FPS from the first frame, the task instruction and the ground-truth
action trajectory, and shown at the  480 × 640 480\times 640  frame size used for
scoring. Top: the arm picks a bottle from the conveyor and packs it into a
cardboard box already holding other items. Bottom: the arm places a slice of
bread onto the plate beside the toaster.

Table 12:  Training data mixture, measured from dataset metadata rather than from
upstream release figures. Hours are derived as
 frames / fps / 3600 \text{frames}/\text{fps}/3600  and so are consistent with the frame counts
by construction. The mixture spans 20 dataset families, 1,773 LeRobot
repositories, 1.52M episodes and 22 distinct robot platforms; it is
84% real by trajectory time.  Real  and  Sim  split
each family by data source, and two families contribute both.
Table 13 :  Model architecture.
Table 14 :  Midtraining hyperparameters. The architecture is initialized from the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B checkpoint, whose own training is not reported here.

Table 15 :  Stage 1 autoregressive modelling hyperparameters. The model is
initialized from the midtrained PrimeSim checkpoint and adapted to
chunk-causal generation using teacher forcing.

Table 16 :  Stage 2 causal consistency distillation hyperparameters. Stage 2
initializes both teacher and student from the Stage 1 causal model and
distills the 50-step teacher into a four-step causal student using one online
teacher ODE step per iteration.

Table 17 :  Stage 3 asymmetric distribution matching distillation
hyperparameters. Stage 3 initializes the generator from the four-step causal
student produced by Stage 2 and refines it using a frozen bidirectional
midtrained model as the real-score teacher and a trainable fake-score network
that tracks the student’s generated distribution.

Table 18 :  Stage 4 episode-level rollout and hierarchical temporal memory
hyperparameters. Cache capacities are measured in temporal latent slots.

Table 19 :  Timing environment. All reported numbers use a single GPU at batch
size one.
Table 20 :  Warm-up schedule, timed repetitions and aggregation per model.

Table 21 :  Chunk semantics per model: conditioning history, future frames per
chunk  T T , number of camera views  V V  and denoising steps.

Table 22 :  Approximate latent tokens per forward (Eq.  14 ).
GE-Sim 2.0 counts its effective temporal extent including memory; Ctrl-World
uses its stacked  576 × 320 576\times 320  canvas; CausalWM’s temporal stride may
differ, so its value is an estimate.
